Q7283727.title: Raid on Scone
paras: In 1296 Edward I of England deposed King John Balliol and ruled Scotland through his own officials. One of them was William de Ormesby, an English judge made Justice of Scotland when Earl Warenne became warden of the conquered kingdom. Edward ordered him to take oaths of homage and fealty from Scotland's landholders, and Ormesby did so with notorious severity, driving those who refused into exile.

In the spring of 1297 the Scots rose against English rule in several places at once. After killing the English sheriff of Lanark in May, William Wallace joined forces with Sir William Douglas, 'the Hardy', and the two led a raid on Scone, the old royal centre near Perth where Ormesby then was. Ormesby was warned at the last moment and escaped with great difficulty, but he had to leave all his property behind as spoil for the raiders. The Scots took control of Scone.

The raid was both practical and symbolic: it drove the chief English law officer out of the heart of the kingdom and struck at the place where Scottish kings had been inaugurated. Sources differ on the month: the Wikipedia article on the raid dates it to June 1297, while the Dictionary of National Biography and the Wikipedia article on Ormesby place it at the outbreak of Wallace's revolt in May.

Douglas was soon captured by the English after the Scottish nobles' capitulation at Irvine, but Wallace kept fighting. Joining Andrew Moray, who had raised the north, he won the Battle of Stirling Bridge on 11 September 1297 and became Guardian of Scotland. Ormesby survived to serve Edward I in England, raising foot soldiers in October 1297 after the defeat at Stirling.

Q83224.title: Battle of Hastings
Q83224.place: Near Hastings, Sussex (today Battle, East Sussex)
paras: The battle was fought on 14 October 1066 between the English army of King Harold Godwinson and the invading army of William, Duke of Normandy, with commanders such as William fitzOsbern and Eustace II of Boulogne. Modern estimates put each army at somewhere between about 5,000 and 13,000 men; contemporary Norman figures are wildly exaggerated.

It was a war of succession. Edward the Confessor died childless on 5 January 1066 and Harold was crowned, but Duke William claimed that Edward had promised him the throne, and King Harald Hardrada of Norway also claimed it. Hardrada invaded the north with Harold's exiled brother Tostig; Harold destroyed their army at Stamford Bridge on 25 September. Three days later, on 28 September, William landed at Pevensey on the south coast and fortified Hastings, forcing Harold to march south again.

Fighting began in the morning and lasted until dusk. The English stood in a shield wall along a ridge; Norman archers shooting uphill and attacks by infantry and mounted knights failed to break it. When part of William's army fell back and a rumour spread that he was dead, William rode among his men to show himself and turned the retreat into a counter-attack against the English who had pursued them. Norman chroniclers say the Normans then used feigned flights to draw more men out of the line; most historians accept this, though some think it a later embellishment. Late in the day Harold was killed, and his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine also died.

How Harold died is uncertain. The famous arrow in the eye rests on a later tradition and an ambiguous scene of the Bayeux Tapestry, which was restored in the 19th century; the earliest written mention of the arrow dates from the 1080s, and other accounts say he was cut down by knights.

The victory did not end English resistance at once, but after William marched on London the English leaders submitted to him at Berkhamsted, and he was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066. Rebellions continued for years, answered by the Harrying of the North in 1069-1070. William founded Battle Abbey on the site.

Q12519.title: Magna Carta
Q12519.place: Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines (Kingdom of England)
paras: Magna Carta was the peace settlement between King John of England and a party of rebel barons. Its text is dated 15 June 1215 at the meadow of Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines; talks had begun there on 10 June, and on 19 June John announced to his officials that peace had been restored. Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, mediated and helped turn the barons' written demands, the 'Articles of the Barons', into the charter.

The crisis grew out of John's failed wars to recover the lands in France he had lost to Philip II, ending in defeat at Bouvines in 1214. To pay for them John squeezed his barons with heavy feudal charges: records in the royal accounts show one baron paying 10,000 marks in inheritance tax in 1214 and another promising 20,000 marks for permission to marry. In May 1215 the rebels renounced their allegiance and took London, forcing John to negotiate.

The charter promised to protect the rights of the Church, to stop imprisonment without lawful judgement, to give swift justice and to limit the King's feudal payments, some of them only with the consent of the realm. Clause 61, the 'security clause', set up a council of 25 barons who could seize the King's castles and lands if he failed to put right a breach within 40 days; John ordered everyone to swear an oath to these 25.

The peace failed within weeks. Both sides had appealed to Pope Innocent III, John's overlord since 1213, and the Pope annulled the charter, which led to the First Barons' War. After John's death the regents of the young Henry III reissued a shortened charter in 1216 and again in 1217, when it first took the name Magna Carta; Henry III reissued it in 1225 in return for a tax, and Edward I confirmed it as statute in 1297.

Its fame came later. In the 17th century Sir Edward Coke used it against the claims of the Stuart kings, and the idea of ancient English liberties it came to stand for influenced the American colonists. Most historians now stress that in 1215 it dealt with the King and his barons rather than with the rights of ordinary people. Most of it has been repealed, but three clauses are still law in England and Wales.

Q160077.title: Fall of Constantinople
paras: On 29 May 1453 the army of the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II took Constantinople, capital of the Byzantine Empire, after a siege that had begun on 6 April. The city was defended by Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos with Greek troops and Italian volunteers, among them the Genoese commander Giovanni Giustiniani, who led the defence of the land walls. Numbers are uncertain: modern estimates put the defenders at about 7,000-8,000 against an Ottoman army of perhaps 50,000-80,000.

By 1453 the empire had shrunk to little more than the city and a few outlying territories, its population thinned by plague and economic decline. The city had fallen only once before, to the Fourth Crusade in 1204. In 1452 Mehmed built the fortress of Rumeli Hisarı on the Bosphorus to control shipping to the city, and the West sent only small groups of volunteers; no large relief fleet arrived in time.

Ottoman bombards, including the great cannon cast by the engineer Orban, battered the ancient land walls, which the defenders repaired after each bombardment. A chain across the Golden Horn kept the Ottoman fleet out of the harbour until Mehmed had ships dragged overland on greased logs into the Horn. Ottoman mines under the walls were destroyed by Byzantine counter-mines. Constantine refused an offer to surrender. The final assault began after midnight on 29 May; when Giustiniani was badly wounded and carried away, the defence broke and the Ottomans entered the city.

Constantine XI died that day; how he died is not known for certain, and most accounts say he fell fighting in the streets. The city was sacked, and many inhabitants were killed or enslaved. Mehmed entered Hagia Sophia, which was turned into the city's chief mosque, and made Constantinople the Ottoman capital in place of Adrianople (Edirne).

The fall ended the Byzantine Empire, the last remnant of the Roman state. Many Greek scholars fled to Italy, taking Byzantine learning with them, and many historians use the year as a marker for the end of the Middle Ages.

Q6539.title: Storming of the Bastille
paras: On 14 July 1789 a crowd of armed Parisians, joined in the afternoon by mutinous soldiers of the French Guards, attacked and took the Bastille, a medieval fortress and state prison in eastern Paris. It was held by its governor, Bernard-René Jourdan de Launay, with about 82 invalides (veteran soldiers) and 32 Swiss grenadiers, while several thousand royal troops camped on the Champ de Mars did not intervene.

France was in financial crisis and the Estates-General, called in May 1789, had turned into a National Assembly in June. On 11 July Louis XVI dismissed his popular minister Jacques Necker, and Parisians feared that troops massing around the city would be used to crush the Assembly. On 13 July the electors of Paris formed a citizens' militia, and on the morning of the 14th a crowd seized tens of thousands of muskets at the Invalides but found no powder. Some 250 barrels of gunpowder had been moved to the Bastille, which is why the crowd went there.

Delegates from the city hall negotiated inside the fortress through the morning while the crowd grew. Around 1:30 p.m. attackers broke into the outer courtyard and cut the chains of a drawbridge, and shooting began. After 3 p.m. French Guards arrived with cannon. At about 5 p.m. de Launay stopped the firing and threatened to blow up the powder unless his men could leave; at about 5:30, short of food and water, he opened the gates. Around a hundred attackers and one defender were killed in the fighting; sources give slightly different totals.

De Launay was taken towards the Hôtel de Ville and killed by the crowd on the way, and the city's provost Jacques de Flesselles was also killed. Inside, the attackers freed only seven prisoners: four forgers, a man described as a lunatic, a man who had tried to kill Louis XV decades before, and a count held at his family's request.

The King recalled Necker, and on 17 July in Paris accepted the revolutionary cockade; Lafayette took command of the new National Guard. Nobles began to emigrate and the 'Great Fear' spread through the countryside. The Bastille was demolished within months, and 14 July became France's national day. Historians debate whether it was the Revolution's real starting point, but it became its great symbol.

Q1025466.title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
paras: On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BC, Gaius Julius Caesar was stabbed to death at a meeting of the Senate in the Curia of Pompey, part of Pompey's theatre complex in Rome. The ancient sources speak of about 60 conspirators, senators led by Marcus Junius Brutus, Gaius Cassius Longinus, Decimus Junius Brutus Albinus and Gaius Trebonius; Decimus posted gladiators nearby in the Portico of Pompey.

Caesar had won the civil war against Pompey and his allies and early in 44 BC was made dictator for life (dictator perpetuo). Many senators believed he meant to make himself king: Livy lists as last straws his failure to rise when a Senate delegation came to him, his removal of two tribunes after a diadem was placed on his statue, and the diadem Mark Antony offered him at the Lupercalia, which he refused. The conspirators called themselves defenders of the Republic.

As Caesar took his seat, Tillius Cimber came up as if to plead for his exiled brother and seized Caesar's toga; Caesar cried out that this was violence. One of the Casca brothers struck first, and the others joined in. Suetonius, writing about 160 years later, says Caesar received 23 wounds, and that the physician Antistius judged only the second, in the chest, to be fatal. Suetonius says he died without a word, only a groan, though some wrote that he said in Greek to Brutus, 'You too, my child?'; 'Et tu, Brute?' is Shakespeare's line. Three slaves carried the body home on a litter.

The killing did not restore the Republic. Mark Antony arranged a compromise under which the assassins went unpunished but Caesar's acts stayed valid. Caesar's will made his grandnephew Octavian his heir; in November 43 BC Octavian, Antony and Lepidus formed the Second Triumvirate, proscribed their enemies and defeated Brutus and Cassius at Philippi in 42 BC, the year Caesar was declared a god. Octavian, as Augustus from 27 BC, became the first Roman emperor.

Q221474.title: Columbus reaches the Americas (first voyage)
Q221474.place: The Bahamas, Cuba and Hispaniola (sailing for the Crown of Castile)
paras: Christopher Columbus, a Genoese navigator, sailed in the service of the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile. Under the Capitulations of Santa Fe, signed on 17 April 1492, they made him Admiral of the Ocean Sea and governor of any lands he found, with a share of their revenue. He planned to reach Asia by sailing west.

Three ships left Palos on 3 August 1492: the Santa María, owned by Juan de la Cosa and commanded by Columbus, the Pinta under Martín Alonso Pinzón and the Niña under Vicente Yáñez Pinzón, crewed largely by local volunteers recruited by Pinzón. After repairs and provisioning in the Canary Islands they left La Gomera on 6 September. Land was sighted in the night of 11 October and on 12 October they landed on an island its Taíno inhabitants called Guanahani, which Columbus named San Salvador; which modern island it was is disputed, though San Salvador Island in the Bahamas is the most likely. The seaman Rodrigo de Triana first sighted land, though Columbus later claimed the reward.

The fleet sailed on through the Bahamas, reached Cuba on 28 October and Hispaniola in early December, looking for gold; Columbus's own log tells of natives taken from San Salvador as guides. On 25 December the Santa María ran aground off Hispaniola and was wrecked; about 39 men were left at a fort called La Navidad, built from its timbers. The Niña and Pinta started home on 16 January 1493 and, after storms, a stop in the Azores and a call at Lisbon, reached Palos on 15 March 1493.

Columbus believed to the end that he had reached the edge of Asia. In 1493 the papal bull Inter caetera assigned the new lands to Castile, and in 1494 the Treaty of Tordesillas divided the non-European world between Spain and Portugal. The voyage began lasting European colonisation of the Americas and the exchange of plants and animals between the two hemispheres. Norse Greenlanders had reached Newfoundland about 500 years earlier, without lasting consequence.

Q179684.title: Spanish Armada
Q179684.place: The English Channel and the coast of Flanders
paras: In 1588 Philip II of Spain sent a great fleet, the Armada, to sweep the English Channel and escort the Duke of Parma's army from Flanders across to invade England. He meant to overthrow the Protestant Elizabeth I, end English support for the Dutch rebels and stop English privateers raiding Spanish ships and colonies. The execution of the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots, in February 1587 hardened his resolve, and Francis Drake's raid on Cádiz in April 1587 set the preparations back by about a year.

The fleet was commanded by the Duke of Medina Sidonia, a capable administrator with no experience at sea, appointed after the death of the admiral Santa Cruz. It left Lisbon with about 130 ships and close to 30,000 sailors and soldiers. The English fleet, under Lord Howard of Effingham with Drake and John Hawkins, had more ships but they were smaller and handier.

The Armada was sighted off the Lizard in Cornwall on 29 July (New Style). In a week of running fights off Plymouth, Portland and the Isle of Wight neither side did much damage, though the Spanish lost the flagship Nuestra Señora del Rosario, captured with its commander Pedro de Valdés. On 7 August the Armada anchored off Calais to wait for Parma, whose army was not ready. That night the English sent in eight fireships; none set a Spanish ship alight, but the Spanish cut their cables and scattered. The next day, 8 August, the English attacked the broken formation off Gravelines and sank or captured several ships.

A wind change saved the fleet from running onto the Flemish banks, but it could not return through the Channel and sailed home round Scotland and Ireland, where storms wrecked many ships. Estimates of the losses differ: Wikipedia gives about 44 ships lost and 11,000-20,000 dead, many from disease; other accounts say as many as half the fleet. Elizabeth's victory became a national legend, but the Anglo-Spanish War went on until 1604, and an English counter-armada in 1589 failed as badly.

cp05-01.title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
cp05-01.place: Wittenberg, Electorate of Saxony (Holy Roman Empire)
paras: On 31 October 1517 Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and professor of theology at the University of Wittenberg in Electoral Saxony, sent a set of 95 Latin theses for academic debate to Albert, Archbishop of Mainz, under whose authority indulgences were being sold in the region.

The theses attacked the preaching and sale of indulgences, certificates said to reduce the punishment for sins after death. Johann Tetzel was selling them in a campaign whose proceeds went partly to rebuilding St Peter's Basilica in Rome. Luther argued that a truly repentant Christian already had full remission of penalty and guilt without indulgence letters, and that preachers who promised more misled the faithful.

The famous picture of Luther nailing the theses to the door of All Saints' Church in Wittenberg comes from a later account by his colleague Philip Melanchthon; Luther's own statements do not mention it, and historians debate whether it happened. What is certain is that the theses spread fast through print: several hundred Latin copies were printed in Germany in 1517, as pamphlets and placards in Basel, Leipzig and Nuremberg.

Theologians such as Johann Eck and Tetzel answered in print, and the Leipzig Debate of 1519 deepened the quarrel with Eck. The papal bull Exsurge Domine (1520) threatened him with excommunication; Luther burned it and was excommunicated in 1521. The theses are generally taken as the start of the Protestant Reformation, though Luther later said he was still a loyal 'papist' when he wrote them.

Q150995.title: Peace of Westphalia
Q150995.place: Münster and Osnabrück, Westphalia (Holy Roman Empire)
paras: The Peace of Westphalia is the name for the treaties signed at Osnabrück and Münster, the main ones concluded on 24 October 1648, that ended the Thirty Years' War in the Holy Roman Empire. The parties were the Emperor Ferdinand III, France, Sweden, their allies and the princes and cities of the Empire. Delegations had gathered in the two Westphalian towns from 1643 onwards.

A separate Peace of Münster between Spain and the Dutch Republic, signed on 30 January 1648, ended the Eighty Years' War and recognised Dutch independence. The Swiss Confederacy was recognised as legally independent of the Empire.

The settlement redrew the religious rules of the Empire: Calvinism was recognised alongside Catholicism and Lutheranism, 1 January 1624 became the 'normative date' that fixed which confession each territory kept, and subjects were no longer simply required to follow their ruler's faith. France received sovereignty over the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun and lands in Alsace; Sweden gained Western Pomerania, Wismar, the bishoprics of Bremen and Verden and an indemnity of five million thalers; Brandenburg gained Farther Pomerania; the Palatinate was divided with Bavaria.

Older histories treated the peace as the founding of a modern system of sovereign states. Most historians now call that the 'Westphalian myth': the treaty texts say nothing of the kind, and the Emperor lost less power than once claimed.

Q48314.title: Battle of Waterloo
Q48314.place: Near Waterloo, south of Brussels (United Kingdom of the Netherlands; today Belgium)
paras: The Battle of Waterloo was fought on 18 June 1815 about 12 miles (20 km) south of Brussels, in what was then the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. Napoleon's French Army of the North, roughly 72,000-74,500 men, attacked an Anglo-allied army of about 68,000 under the Duke of Wellington, while a Prussian army of about 50,000 under Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher marched to join it. It was Napoleon's last battle.

Napoleon had taken power again in France in March 1815, beginning the 'Hundred Days'. Facing a Seventh Coalition, he struck first in the Low Countries, hoping to beat the British-led and Prussian armies separately before they could combine. On 16 June he defeated Blücher at Ligny while Wellington held Quatre Bras; he then sent about a third of his army, some 33,000 men, after the retreating Prussians, and that force was held up at Wavre and never reached Waterloo. Wellington drew up on a ridge near Mont-Saint-Jean.

Through the afternoon of 18 June Wellington's line withstood repeated French infantry and cavalry attacks. Around 6 p.m. Marshal Ney's troops took the farmhouse of La Haye Sainte in the allied centre, but Napoleon, distracted by the Prussians now attacking his eastern flank, did not reinforce him until after 7 p.m. By then Wellington had reorganised. Napoleon's last reserve, the Imperial Guard, attacked and was driven back; the allied army advanced along the whole line as the Prussians broke through on the French right, and the French army dissolved into rout.

Wellington's army lost about 17,000 men and Blücher's about 7,000; the French lost about 25,000 killed or wounded and some 8,000-9,000 captured. Napoleon abdicated four days later, and coalition troops entered Paris on 7 July. Waterloo ended the Hundred Days and the First French Empire; Napoleon spent his last years as a British prisoner on Saint Helena.

Q192050.title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
paras: On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, were shot dead in Sarajevo, capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which Austria-Hungary had annexed in 1908. The killer was Gavrilo Princip, a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb student.

Princip belonged to a group of young Bosnian conspirators linked to the Young Bosnia movement, which wanted to end Austro-Hungarian rule and unite the South Slavs. The Serbian secret society known as the Black Hand, whose leaders included the army officer Dragutin Dimitrijević ('Apis'), helped arm and train them, and the weapons were smuggled into Bosnia along a secret route. Each conspirator carried bombs or pistols and a cyanide capsule. Princip later said he also wanted to stop the reforms the Archduke planned, which might have strengthened the Slavic lands within the empire.

That morning, at about 10:15, one conspirator, Nedeljko Čabrinović, threw a bomb at the motorcade on its way to a reception at the city hall; it missed the Archduke's car and wounded about 16 to 20 people. After the reception the party set off again, the driver took a wrong turn, and as the car stopped nearby Princip stepped up and fired at close range. Both the Archduke and his wife died.

The killing set off the July Crisis: Austria-Hungary, blaming Serbia, declared war on it, and the alliance system turned that war into the First World War. Anti-Serb riots broke out in Sarajevo. Princip, too young at 19 for the death penalty, was sentenced to 20 years and died of tuberculosis in prison; older co-conspirators were hanged. In 1917 a Serbian court at Salonika tried Apis and other Black Hand leaders on charges now widely seen as fabricated, and executed them.

Q42976.title: October Revolution
paras: In the October Revolution the Bolshevik party, led by Vladimir Lenin, seized power in Petrograd from Russia's Provisional Government on 25-26 October 1917 by the Julian calendar then used in Russia, 7-8 November by the Gregorian. The rising was organised by the Military Revolutionary Committee of the Petrograd Soviet, which the Soviet had set up three weeks before the Congress of Soviets on a resolution of Leon Trotsky.

The February Revolution had brought down Tsar Nicholas II, but the Provisional Government, led by Alexander Kerensky, kept Russia in the unpopular world war amid food shortages and economic collapse. Workers and soldiers organised in soviets, and the Bolsheviks won support with anti-war slogans and the demand 'All power to the soviets'. After the July Days the party was repressed and Lenin went into hiding, but the failed Kornilov affair, a right-wing military move on Petrograd, led to the release of Bolsheviks including Trotsky and strengthened them. On 10 October (Old Style) the Bolshevik Central Committee voted for an armed rising.

On 24-25 October, after the government moved to close Bolshevik newspapers, Bolshevik forces under the Military Revolutionary Committee occupied the bridges, the telegraph office and other key points; the cruiser Aurora fired a signal shot. In the early hours of 26 October they entered the Winter Palace, where the government's ministers were, and arrested them, meeting little resistance; Kerensky had already left. The dramatic battle for the palace shown in later Soviet re-enactments and films largely did not happen.

The Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets, with a Bolshevik majority, approved the seizure of power; Mensheviks and right Socialist Revolutionaries walked out. It set up a Council of People's Commissars (Sovnarkom) headed by Lenin and adopted the Decree on Peace and the Decree on Land; further decrees nationalised banks and factories and brought in the eight-hour day. When elections to the Constituent Assembly gave the Bolsheviks only about a quarter of the seats, they dissolved it after its first sitting in January 1918. Civil war followed, ending in 1922 with the founding of the Soviet Union. Soviet historians presented the revolution as a popular uprising; many Western historians have called it a coup.

Q488.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
paras: On 6 and 9 August 1945 the United States dropped atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. They were the product of the Manhattan Project. The Hiroshima bomb, 'Little Boy', was a uranium gun-type weapon dropped from the B-29 Enola Gay, commanded by Paul Tibbets; the Nagasaki bomb, 'Fat Man', was a plutonium implosion weapon, carried by the B-29 Bockscar under Charles Sweeney.

On 26 July the Allies' Potsdam Declaration demanded Japan's unconditional surrender and threatened 'prompt and utter destruction'; the Japanese government ignored it. Orders of 25 July listed Hiroshima, Kokura, Niigata and Nagasaki as targets.

Over Hiroshima on the morning of 6 August, Little Boy exploded about 1,900 feet above the city, close to where soldiers of the Japanese Second Army were exercising. President Truman announced the new weapon that day and warned of more if Japan did not surrender. On 9 August Bockscar's primary target was the arsenal city of Kokura, but it was hidden by smoke and haze; short of fuel, the crew turned to the secondary target, Nagasaki, where the bombardier dropped the bomb after glimpsing the city through the clouds.

Estimates of the dead by the end of 1945 range from 90,000 to 166,000 in Hiroshima and 60,000 to 80,000 in Nagasaki; an official US history estimates some 70,000 deaths in Hiroshima from the immediate effects of blast, heat and radiation. In the same days the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and invaded Manchuria. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August and signed the instrument of surrender on 2 September 1945. Whether the bombings were necessary to end the war, or were a war crime, is still debated.

Q43653.title: Apollo 11
Q43653.place: Launched from Kennedy Space Center, Florida (United States); landed in the Sea of Tranquility on the Moon
paras: Apollo 11 was the NASA mission that first landed people on the Moon. A Saturn V rocket launched it from Launch Complex 39A at the Kennedy Space Center on 16 July 1969 with Neil Armstrong as commander, Michael Collins as command module pilot and Edwin 'Buzz' Aldrin as lunar module pilot.

It answered the goal President John F. Kennedy set on 25 May 1961: to land a man on the Moon and return him safely to Earth before the end of the decade. The Soviet Union had led the early Space Race, launching the first satellite, Sputnik 1, in October 1957 and the first person in space, Yuri Gagarin, in April 1961.

On 20 July, Armstrong and Aldrin separated in the lunar module Eagle from the command module Columbia, which Collins kept in lunar orbit. Partly flown by hand by Armstrong, Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility at 20:17 UTC. About six hours later Armstrong stepped onto the surface, saying 'That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind'; Aldrin followed 19 minutes later. An estimated 650 million people watched on television. Their moonwalk lasted about two and a half hours, and they collected about 21.5 kg of lunar rock and soil.

After more than 21 hours on the surface, Eagle's ascent stage rejoined Columbia, and the crew splashed down in the Pacific on 24 July 1969, where USS Hornet picked them up. The landing fulfilled Kennedy's goal; a Soviet probe, Luna 15, crashed on the Moon on 21 July while Apollo 11 was there.

Q8707.title: Meiji Restoration
paras: The Meiji Restoration was the overthrow of the Tokugawa shogunate, the military government of the shōguns, and the return of practical power to the emperor. On 3 January 1868 Emperor Meiji declared political power restored to the Imperial House. The movement was led by the domains of Satsuma and Chōshū.

The shogunate was weakened by economic and political strains and by foreign pressure. In July 1853 the American Commodore Matthew Perry sailed four warships into Tokyo (Edo) Bay to force Japan to open regular trade with the West, which it had kept to a minimum for over two hundred years; the shogunate's acceptance of treaties on foreign terms, the 'unequal treaties', divided the samurai. Many rallied to the slogan sonnō jōi, 'revere the emperor, expel the barbarians'.

Supporters of the Tokugawa fought on in the Boshin War of 1868-1869 and briefly in the Republic of Ezo, but by the early 1870s the emperor's government was unchallenged. Its aims were set out in the Charter Oath of 1868. In a few years it replaced the old currency, abolished the feudal domains and ended the privileged status of the samurai, and it set out to build industry and an army on Western models. Discontented samurai rose against these changes in the Saga Rebellion and the Satsuma Rebellion.

The Meiji Constitution of 1889 gave the new Empire of Japan its framework until the Allied occupation after the Second World War. Industrialised on Western lines, Japan went on to pursue colonial interests in East Asia. At the time it was called goishin, the 'honourable restoration'; it has also been translated as the Meiji Reformation.

Q127912.title: United States Declaration of Independence
paras: On 4 July 1776 the Second Continental Congress, meeting in the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia, approved the Declaration of Independence, announcing that the thirteen American colonies regarded themselves as independent states no longer under British rule.

The vote for independence itself came two days earlier. On 7 June 1776 Richard Henry Lee of Virginia, following instructions from the Virginia Convention of 15 May, moved that 'these United Colonies are, and of right ought to be, free and independent States'. Congress postponed the decision, but appointed a Committee of Five to draft a statement of the colonies' case: John Adams of Massachusetts, Roger Sherman of Connecticut, Benjamin Franklin of Pennsylvania, Robert R. Livingston of New York and Thomas Jefferson of Virginia. On 2 July Congress adopted Lee's resolution by the votes of 12 colonies, with New York abstaining.

Jefferson wrote the first draft; Adams and Franklin made a few changes, and Congress then cut the text by about a quarter, removing Jefferson's passage blaming King George III for imposing slavery on the colonies. The final text listed 27 grievances against the King. Printed broadsides by John Dunlap spread it across the colonies; a handwritten 'engrossed' copy, ordered on 19 July, was signed mostly on 2 August 1776, eventually by 56 delegates.
It became the founding statement of the United States. Abraham Lincoln later treated it as the nation's moral standard and built the Gettysburg Address around it.

Q362.title: World War II
Q362.place: Worldwide (Europe, Asia and the Pacific, Africa, the Atlantic)
paras: The Second World War, from 1 September 1939 to 2 September 1945, was fought between two coalitions: the Allies and the Axis powers. Nearly every country in the world was drawn in, and much of it was fought as total war. It was the deadliest conflict in history: estimates of the dead run from about 60 million to 75 million, most of them civilians, who died in massacres, starvation, disease and genocides.

Its causes lay in the unresolved tensions left by the First World War and in the rise of fascism in Europe and militarism in Japan. Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931 and went to war with China in 1937; Germany annexed Austria and the Sudetenland. On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded Poland, and two days later Britain and France declared war on Germany; the Soviet Union, bound to Germany by the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, invaded Poland from the east in mid-September and the two divided it.

In 1940 Germany conquered Norway, Denmark, the Low Countries and France, while the Soviet Union annexed the Baltic states and parts of Finland and Romania; Britain and its Commonwealth fought on, in the air over Britain, at sea in the Atlantic and in North Africa and the Mediterranean. On 22 June 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union. In December 1941 Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and British and American territories in the Pacific, bringing the United States into the war. The tide turned in 1942-1943: at Midway in June 1942, in North Africa, and at Stalingrad, where a Soviet counter-offensive from November 1942 destroyed a German army.

The Allies invaded Italy in 1943, bringing down Mussolini's regime, and landed in Normandy in June 1944 while the Soviet army advanced into Central Europe. Berlin fell and Germany surrendered unconditionally on 8 May 1945. After the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria in August, Japan announced its surrender on 15 August and signed it on 2 September 1945. Germany, Austria, Japan and Korea were occupied, German and Japanese leaders were tried for war crimes, and the United Nations was founded; the war left the United States and the Soviet Union as rival superpowers.

Q361.title: World War I
Q361.place: Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia and the oceans
paras: The First World War, or Great War, lasted from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918. It was fought between the Allies (the Entente) and the Central Powers, and caused some 15 to 22 million deaths, including those from war crimes and genocides; it also helped spread the 1918 influenza pandemic. It brought machine guns, artillery, aircraft, poison gas and tanks into large-scale use.

Its deeper causes were the rise of the German Empire, which upset the balance of power in Europe, and the sharpening of imperial rivalries through new alliances and an arms race. The spark came on 28 June 1914, when the Bosnian Serb Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war on it on 28 July; Russia mobilised to defend Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia and France in early August, and Britain entered after Germany invaded Belgium.

Germany's plan to defeat France quickly was stopped in September 1914, and the Western Front settled into lines of trenches. The great battles of Verdun and the Somme in 1916, and Passchendaele, failed to break the deadlock; at Verdun alone German and French casualties approached a million. The Eastern Front was more fluid but indecisive. The Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers in November 1914, and an Allied landing at Gallipoli failed; Japan and Italy joined the Allies. In April 1917 the United States entered the war after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare; American opinion had already been turned by the sinking of the liner Lusitania in May 1915.

After the October Revolution, Soviet Russia made an armistice in December 1917 and a separate peace in March 1918. Germany's spring offensive of 1918 exhausted its army, and the Allied Hundred Days Offensive from August broke the German front. The Ottomans and Austria-Hungary signed armistices in early November; facing revolution at home, Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated on 9 November, and the Armistice of 11 November ended the fighting.

The Paris Peace Conference of 1919-1920 imposed the peace treaties: under the Treaty of Versailles Germany lost territory, was disarmed and had to pay reparations. The German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and Russian empires collapsed, and new states arose, among them Poland, Finland, the Baltic states, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia. The League of Nations was set up to keep the peace; its failure to manage the instability of the interwar years contributed to the Second World War.

Q608613.title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
paras: By convention the Western Roman Empire ended on 4 September 476, when Odoacer, a Germanic leader of the mercenaries in Italy, deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus and made himself ruler of Italy; the Roman Senate sent the imperial insignia to the Eastern emperor Zeno in Constantinople. The date marks the end of a long process in which the Western Empire lost central control of its provinces, which were divided among successor kingdoms.

Historians give many causes: the size and effectiveness of the army, the health and numbers of the population, the economy, the competence of emperors, civil wars, religious change and the efficiency of the administration, together with growing pressure from peoples outside the empire, worsened by climate change and epidemics. In 376 a large body of Goths fleeing the Huns entered the empire and could not be expelled or subdued. When Theodosius I died in 395 the empire was divided between his two sons, and from then on the Western army became small and ineffective.

Barbarian groups crossed the Rhine and other frontiers. The Visigoth king Alaric sacked Rome in 410, the Vandals took North Africa and sacked Rome again in 455, and Germanic peoples occupied Britain and Spain. By the 470s Western emperors were puppets of military strongmen. In 475 the general Orestes drove out the emperor Julius Nepos and proclaimed his young son Romulus emperor; 'Augustulus', 'little Augustus', was his rivals' mockery. When Orestes refused land in Italy to his Heruli, Scirian and Torcilingi mercenaries, they revolted under Odoacer, and in 476 Odoacer deposed Romulus.

The convention has many qualifications. Julius Nepos still claimed to be emperor in Dalmatia until he was murdered in 480, and Syagrius ruled a Roman remnant at Soissons until 486. The Eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire survived for centuries more, and the legitimacy and culture of Rome long outlived the Western Empire.

Q700983.title: German Instrument of Surrender
paras: Germany's unconditional surrender, which ended the Second World War in Europe, was signed twice. In the early hours of Monday 7 May 1945, at General Eisenhower's headquarters (SHAEF) in Reims in north-eastern France, General Alfred Jodl, chief of staff of the German army, signed for the German High Command. The Allied delegation was led by Eisenhower's chief of staff, Walter Bedell Smith, with Soviet and French representatives present; Eisenhower refused to meet the Germans until the surrender had been signed.

Germany was then governed by Grand Admiral Karl Dönitz, whom Hitler had named head of state in his testament before killing himself in his bunker on 30 April 1945. Berlin fell two days later. After the Reims signing the German forces were ordered to stop fighting in the west but to go on fighting in the east, and the Soviet command protested that the Reims document looked like a separate peace. It demanded that the surrender be signed again in Berlin, the seat of the government from which the war had been launched.

So on 8 May, in Berlin, a second document, only slightly changed from the Reims text, was signed with Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel as the senior German representative, before representatives of the Allied Expeditionary Force and the Soviet High Command, with French and American witnesses. It was signed at 22:43 Central European Time and took effect at 23:01 the same day. For the Soviet Union, the Berlin document was the official, legal surrender of the Third Reich.

The surrender was military only. On 5 June 1945 the four Allies (the Soviet Union, the United States, the United Kingdom and France) declared in the Berlin Declaration that Germany had no government and that they had assumed supreme authority over it, the basis of the Allied occupation.

cp03-01.title: Temüjin is proclaimed Genghis Khan
paras: In 1206 a great assembly of the Mongols, a kurultai, met at the source of the Onon River and proclaimed the warlord Temüjin ruler of all the steppe peoples he had united, with the title Genghis (Chinggis) Khan. He had been born around 1162, the son of the Borjigin chieftain Yesugei; after his father's death, when Temüjin was a boy, the clan abandoned the family and left it close to poverty.

His rise took some twenty years of war and shifting alliances. With his early allies, the steppe leaders Jamukha and Toghrul, he recovered his kidnapped wife Börte; later both became his enemies. Defeated by Jamukha around 1187, he re-emerged in 1196, overcame Toghrul after a surprise attack in 1203, defeated the Naiman, and had Jamukha executed, leaving him sole ruler of the Mongolian steppe.

What 'Genghis' meant is debated: it may simply have set him above the older title gurkhan that Jamukha had held, it may suggest strength or righteousness, or it may come from the Turkic tängiz, 'ocean', making him a universal ruler. After the assembly he reorganised the Mongols to break the power of the tribes: warriors were grouped in units of ten without regard to kinship, and loyalty was owed to the khan and his family, the 'Golden Family'.

The new state turned outward at once: it raided Western Xia in 1209, made war on the Jin dynasty and took the Jin capital Zhongdu (Beijing), and from 1219 destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire after the killing of Genghis's envoys. Genghis Khan died in August 1227 while subduing Western Xia; his son Ögedei succeeded him in 1229.

Q69163529.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
paras: On the evening of 9 November 1989 a spokesman of East Germany's ruling party told a press conference that East Germans could now travel across the border, and that the new rules applied 'immediately, without delay'. The announcement was premature: the new travel law was still being discussed. Broadcast in both East and West, the news brought crowds to the crossing points in Berlin, and in the late evening the puzzled border guards let them through, as television carried the scenes around the world.

The Wall had been built from August 1961; at least 140 people were killed trying to get over, under or around it, and hundreds more died at the fortified inner German border. In 1989 the communist bloc began to open: Hungary removed its border fence in May and opened its border in August, after the Pan-European Picnic of 19 August on the Austro-Hungarian border, and Czechoslovakia let out East Germans who had crowded into the West German embassy in Prague. The flight of East Germans through neighbouring countries put the leadership under pressure, and its long-time leader Erich Honecker was ousted in October.

In the following days thousands crossed, and further crossings were opened; the Wall was later demolished and its concrete segments spread around the world. Having lost control of the border, the East German government soon lost control of the country in the Peaceful Revolution. The first free elections in spring 1990 showed a wish for unification and the West German mark, which came in July; on 3 October 1990 East Germany joined the Federal Republic as five new states, with Berlin reunited.

Q193484.title: Assassination of John F. Kennedy
paras: On Friday 22 November 1963 President John F. Kennedy was shot while riding in an open car in a motorcade through Dallas, Texas, with his wife Jacqueline, Texas governor John Connally and Connally's wife Nellie. The motorcade, planned by Connally and the President's aide Kenneth O'Donnell for a two-day Texas trip, was passing the Texas School Book Depository, a seven-storey warehouse at Houston and Elm Streets, at about 12:30 p.m. when shots were fired from the building.

Kennedy was rushed to Parkland Memorial Hospital, four miles away, and pronounced dead about 30 minutes after the shooting; Connally was badly wounded but recovered. Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson was sworn in as president aboard Air Force One at Dallas Love Field two hours and eight minutes later.

Lee Harvey Oswald, a former US Marine, went home for a pistol, shot dead a Dallas policeman, J. D. Tippit, and was arrested about 70 minutes after the assassination. Two days later, as live television covered his transfer through the basement of Dallas police headquarters, he was shot dead by the nightclub owner Jack Ruby, who was convicted of murder but died in prison in 1967 awaiting a new trial after the verdict was overturned.

After a ten-month inquiry the Warren Commission (1964) concluded that Oswald killed Kennedy and found no evidence that he or Ruby was part of a conspiracy; later federal inquiries agreed. In 1979, however, the House Select Committee on Assassinations concluded that Kennedy was probably killed as the result of a conspiracy, with 'a high probability that two gunmen fired', a finding that rested largely on a police recording. The only trial, brought by the New Orleans district attorney Jim Garrison against Clay Shaw in 1967, ended in acquittal.

Q10806.title: September 11 attacks
Q10806.place: New York City; the Pentagon, Arlington, Virginia; near Shanksville, Pennsylvania (United States)
paras: On 11 September 2001 nineteen hijackers of the Islamist terrorist organisation al-Qaeda seized four commercial airliners over the eastern United States. At 8:46 a.m. the ringleader, Mohamed Atta, flew American Airlines Flight 11 into floors 93 to 99 of the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York; at 9:03 a.m. Marwan al-Shehhi flew United Airlines Flight 175 into floors 77 to 85 of the South Tower. Both towers collapsed within an hour and forty-two minutes, destroying the rest of the complex.

At 9:37 a.m. Hani Hanjour flew American Airlines Flight 77 into the Pentagon, the headquarters of the US Department of Defense in Arlington County, Virginia. On United Airlines Flight 93, hijacked by Ziad Jarrah and believed to be heading for the Capitol or the White House, the passengers learned of the other attacks and fought back; the hijackers crashed the plane into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at 10:03 a.m., about 20 minutes' flying time from Washington.

The attacks killed 2,977 people from 90 nations: 2,753 in New York, 184 at the Pentagon and 40 on Flight 93. All civil air traffic over the United States was grounded, and flights in the air were sent back or diverted to Canada. That evening the CIA told President George W. Bush that al-Qaeda under Osama bin Laden was responsible.

NATO invoked Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty for the only time to date. The United States invaded Afghanistan and launched what it called the Global War on Terror, which later included the invasion of Iraq.

Q6540361.title: Surrender of Japan
paras: Japan's surrender, which ended the Second World War, was announced by Emperor Hirohito on 15 August 1945 and signed on 2 September 1945. By the end of July Japan's navy could no longer conduct major operations and an Allied invasion was imminent. On 26 July the United States, the United Kingdom and China demanded Japan's unconditional surrender in the Potsdam Declaration, the alternative being 'prompt and utter destruction'. Japan's leaders, the 'Big Six' of the Supreme Council for the Direction of the War, publicly vowed to fight on while privately asking the still-neutral Soviet Union to mediate better terms.

The Soviet Union was secretly preparing to attack instead, as it had promised the Allies at the Tehran and Yalta conferences. On 6 August the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, and Truman warned Japan to expect 'a rain of ruin from the air'. Late on 8 August the Soviet Union declared war on Japan, breaking their neutrality pact, and just after midnight invaded Manchuria; hours later a second atomic bomb fell on Nagasaki. Hirohito then told the Supreme Council to accept the Potsdam terms.

After further negotiations and a failed coup by army hardliners, the Emperor's recorded radio address of 15 August announced the surrender. The Allied occupation began on 28 August. On the morning of 2 September, on the deck of the battleship USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay, Foreign Minister Mamoru Shigemitsu signed for the Emperor and government and General Yoshijirō Umezu for the Imperial General Headquarters, and General Douglas MacArthur signed as Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers.

Some isolated Japanese soldiers in Asia and the Pacific refused to surrender for years, a few into the 1970s. The part the atomic bombings played in the surrender, and their ethics, are still debated. The state of war formally ended when the Treaty of San Francisco came into force on 28 April 1952; Japan and the Soviet Union ended theirs by a joint declaration in 1956.

Q5167679.title: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
paras: The Soviet Union was formally dissolved on 26 December 1991. Its collapse had many causes: chronic economic stagnation, the cost of the arms race with the United States and of foreign wars, nationalism and separatism in the fifteen union republics, and the destabilising effects of Mikhail Gorbachev's own reforms, glasnost and perestroika.

The republics pulled away first. Estonia declared its sovereignty on 16 November 1988, and Lithuania was the first to declare independence, in March 1990; in January 1991 violence broke out in Lithuania and Latvia. Gorbachev was squeezed between Boris Yeltsin and the democrats, who wanted faster reform, and hard-line communists who wanted to stop it.

In August 1991 hard-line communists tried to overthrow Gorbachev. The coup failed, but it left him weakened and made Yeltsin, who had defied it from the Russian parliament building, the leading figure; the Communist Party's Central Committee was dissolved, and in the following days and months most republics declared independence, Ukraine and Belarus among the first. On 8 December 1991 the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus signed the Belovezha Accords, declaring that the Soviet Union no longer existed and founding the Commonwealth of Independent States; on 21 December most of the other republics joined the Commonwealth by the Alma-Ata Protocol.

On 25 December Gorbachev resigned as president and handed his powers, including control of the nuclear forces, to Yeltsin as president of Russia; that evening the Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin for the last time and replaced by the Russian tricolour. The next day the upper chamber of the Supreme Soviet formally dissolved the union. Russia became its recognised successor state, and the dissolution marked the end of the Cold War.

Q8676.title: American Civil War
Q8676.place: The United States, mostly the South
paras: The American Civil War, from 12 April 1861 to 26 May 1865, was fought between the Union (the North) and the Confederate States (the South), formed in 1861 by Southern states that seceded from the Union to preserve slavery. Decades of conflict over slavery came to a head when Abraham Lincoln, a Republican who opposed its spread into the western territories, won the presidential election of November 1860. Within three months seven slave states, South Carolina, Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana and Texas, had seceded and seized federal forts and property.

The war began on 12 April 1861, when Confederate artillery bombarded Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour after Lincoln had ordered it resupplied. Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina and Tennessee then joined the Confederacy, which under its president Jefferson Davis numbered eleven states with about a third of the country's population; slave states on the border, such as Missouri, Kentucky and Maryland, did not secede. At the First Battle of Bull Run on 21 July 1861 the Confederates forced the Union army back towards Washington, ending hopes of a quick victory.

In the west the Union made lasting gains, taking New Orleans in 1862; in the east the war was long indecisive. With the Emancipation Proclamation of 1 January 1863 Lincoln declared the slaves in the rebel states free, making abolition a Union war aim. In 1863 the fall of Vicksburg split the Confederacy at the Mississippi, and Robert E. Lee's invasion of the North was defeated at Gettysburg. Ulysses S. Grant, given command of all Union armies in 1864, pressed the Confederacy on every front while a naval blockade tightened; William T. Sherman took Atlanta and marched to the sea at Savannah, and after a ten-month siege of Petersburg the Confederates abandoned their capital, Richmond.

Lee surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House on 9 April 1865. Five days later, on 14 April, Lincoln was shot by the Confederate sympathiser John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theatre in Washington and died the next day. The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery and freed some four million people, and the country entered Reconstruction. Estimates of the soldiers killed range from about 620,000 to 750,000, making it the deadliest war fought on American soil.

Q2763.title: The Holocaust
paras: The Holocaust, in Hebrew the Shoah, was the genocide of the Jews of Europe by Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators. Around six million Jews were murdered, about two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population, which in 1933 numbered some nine million. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum dates the Holocaust era from January 1933, when Hitler and the Nazi Party came to power, to the defeat of Germany in May 1945; the systematic murder itself took place from 1941 to 1945.

Nazi ideology rested on racism, antisemitism and the pursuit of 'living space'. The instability of the Weimar Republic, fear of communism and the shock of the Great Depression made many Germans receptive to it. From 1933 the regime passed anti-Jewish laws and encouraged violence to drive German Jews to emigrate, culminating in the nationwide pogrom of Kristallnacht in November 1938. After the invasion of Poland in September 1939 the occupiers forced Jews into ghettos.

After the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, German forces and local collaborators shot 1.5 to 2 million Jews, first men and prisoners of war, soon women and children too. By early 1942, after the Wannsee Conference chaired by Reinhard Heydrich, the 'Final Solution' to murder all the Jews of Europe was in operation. Jews were deported to extermination camps in occupied Poland, Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Bełżec, Sobibór, Chełmno and Majdanek, where those who survived the journey were killed in gas chambers, while others died in forced-labour camps of starvation, abuse and exhaustion or in medical experiments. The killing was most intense in Operation Reinhard, from March 1942 to November 1943, and most victims died in 1942, but it continued until the end of the war.

Nazi persecution also killed millions of non-Jewish civilians and prisoners of war, among them Roma and Soviet POWs, and the term is sometimes used to include them. After the war many survivors left Europe; relatively few perpetrators were tried, and the reparations paid have fallen short of what was lost.

Q6534.title: French Revolution
paras: The French Revolution is the period of political and social upheaval in France from the meeting of the Estates-General in May 1789 to Napoleon Bonaparte's coup of 18 Brumaire (9 November 1799). Many of its ideas became founding principles of liberal democracy.

Its causes were social, political and financial. France's costly part in the American Revolution and the spending of Louis XVI's court had brought the state close to bankruptcy, and in 1786 the controller-general Calonne proposed a land tax from which the nobility would no longer be exempt. To find money, the King called the Estates-General, which had not met since 1614, for 5 May 1789. The Third Estate, the commoners, quarrelled with the clergy and nobility over voting; on 17 June it declared itself the National Assembly, and three days later its members swore the Tennis Court Oath not to disperse until France had a constitution. On 27 June the King gave way and merged the three orders into the Assembly.

The storming of the Bastille in Paris on 14 July 1789 was followed by radical measures: the abolition of feudalism, state control of the Catholic Church, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Louis XVI's attempted flight to Varennes in June 1791 discredited the monarchy, and defeats in the war that began in April 1792 led to the insurrection of 10 August 1792. The monarchy was abolished and the First Republic proclaimed in September 1792, and the King was executed in January 1793.

After a further revolt in June 1793 power passed to the Committee of Public Safety, dominated by the radical Jacobins under Maximilien Robespierre. In the Reign of Terror about 16,000 people were sentenced by the Revolutionary Tribunal and executed, until the Thermidorian Reaction of July 1794 ended it. The Directory that governed from November 1795 was unstable, and in 1799 the coup of 18 Brumaire set up the Consulate with Napoleon as First Consul.

Q2487.title: Thirty Years' War
Q2487.place: Central Europe, mainly the Holy Roman Empire
paras: The Thirty Years' War, fought mainly in Central Europe from 1618 to 1648, was one of the most destructive wars in European history. An estimated 4.5 to 8 million soldiers and civilians died from fighting, famine and disease, and parts of Germany lost more than half their population.

Its roots lay in the religious divisions of the Holy Roman Empire after the Reformation. The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 had divided the empire between Catholic and Lutheran states, but Protestantism kept spreading beyond those lines, and princes and emperor disputed the limits of imperial power. In 1618 the Protestant nobles of Bohemia, angered by Ferdinand II's restrictions on their religious freedom, threw his representatives out of a window of Prague Castle, the Defenestration of Prague, and rejected him as king, choosing the Protestant Frederick V of the Palatinate instead.

Frederick was soon defeated and deposed, but the fighting spread into the Palatinate and drew in outside powers: Spain and the Dutch Republic, then at war in the Eighty Years' War, and kings seeking land in the empire, Christian IV of Denmark and, from 1630, Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, who came to the aid of the northern Protestants and pushed back the Catholic armies. Until 1635 it was mainly a civil war within the empire, largely ended by the Peace of Prague; but France then entered the war in alliance with Sweden, turning it into a wider struggle against the Habsburgs, Emperor Ferdinand III and Spain.

The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 ended the war. It gave the German states, such as Bavaria and Saxony, greater autonomy, gave Sweden territory in northern Germany, and included Spain's recognition of Dutch independence.

Q8698.title: Great Depression
Q8698.place: Worldwide, beginning in the United States
paras: The Great Depression was the severe worldwide economic slump of 1929 to 1939, marked by mass unemployment and poverty, collapsing industrial output and trade, and bank and business failures around the world. It began in the United States, then the world's largest economy, and the Wall Street crash of October 1929 is usually taken as its start; the United States, Britain and Germany had among the most unemployed.

It followed the boom of the 'Roaring Twenties', when much profit went into speculation on the stock market, banks were lightly regulated, lending was loose and debt widespread. Wages were low and farming was already struggling with drought and falling prices. By 1929 falling spending had begun to cut output and raise unemployment while share prices went on rising. On 24 October, 'Black Thursday', panic selling set a record of 12.9 million shares traded, and on 29 October, 'Black Tuesday', some 16 million; prices kept falling until July 1932.

Waves of bank panics followed from the autumn of 1930. By 1933 unemployment in the United States had reached about 25 percent, about a third of farmers had lost their land and some 9,000 of 25,000 banks had failed; the Dust Bowl drove many from the land. President Herbert Hoover was reluctant to intervene, and the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act he signed in 1930 made matters worse. Franklin D. Roosevelt defeated him in 1932 and from 1933 launched the New Deal programmes of relief and job creation.

Between 1929 and 1932 world output fell by an estimated 15 percent, and that of the United States by about 30 percent. In Germany, which depended heavily on American loans, unemployment rose to nearly 30 percent and fed the political extremism that brought Hitler's Nazi Party to power in 1933. Recovery was uneven: the United States, Germany and Japan began to recover in the mid-1930s, France only later in the decade, and in the American account it was the production boom of the Second World War that finally ended the Depression.

Q8663.title: Korean War
paras: The Korean War, from 25 June 1950 to 27 July 1953, was fought between North Korea, backed by China and the Soviet Union, and South Korea, backed by a United Nations Command led by the United States. Korea, a Japanese colony for 35 years, had been divided in 1945 into Soviet and American occupation zones along the 38th parallel. In 1948 the zones formed rival governments, Kim Il Sung's in Pyongyang and Syngman Rhee's in Seoul, each claiming to be the only legitimate government of Korea, and border clashes were frequent.

On 25 June 1950 about 75,000 North Korean soldiers crossed the 38th parallel. With the Soviet representative absent, the UN Security Council condemned the invasion and called on members to help repel it; troops from 21 countries served under the UN command, about 90 percent of them American. North Korean forces took Seoul on 28 June, and by early August the South Korean and allied forces held only the Pusan Perimeter in the south-east.

On 15 September UN forces under General Douglas MacArthur landed at Inchon near Seoul, cutting the North Korean supply lines; they broke out of the perimeter, retook Seoul, invaded the North in October, took Pyongyang and advanced towards the Yalu River on the Chinese border. On 19 October Chinese 'People's Volunteers' crossed the Yalu, and by December the UN forces had been driven out of the North. The communists took Seoul again in January 1951 but lost it two months later, and the front settled roughly along the 38th parallel.

Armistice talks began in July 1951 but dragged on for two years of attritional fighting, while UN bombing destroyed nearly every major city in the North. The armistice signed on 27 July 1953 provided for an exchange of prisoners and created a demilitarised zone along the front, with a Joint Security Area at Panmunjom. No peace treaty has ever been signed. Estimates of the dead differ: about a million soldiers and 1.5 to 3 million civilians according to the figures cited by Wikipedia, about 5 million soldiers and civilians in all according to HISTORY.com.

Q8740.title: Vietnam War
paras: The Vietnam War, from about 1955 to 30 April 1975, was fought in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia between communist North Vietnam, supported by China and the Soviet Union, and South Vietnam, supported by the United States and other anti-communist countries. It was at once a post-colonial war of national liberation, a civil war and a theatre of the Cold War.

After the Viet Minh defeated France, decisively at Dien Bien Phu in May 1954, the Geneva Conference of July 1954 split Vietnam at the 17th parallel. Ho Chi Minh's communists ruled the North, and an anti-communist government under Ngô Đình Diệm, backed by the United States, took over the South. From 1957 the Viet Cong, a communist front in the South supplied and later directed by the North, stepped up a guerrilla war; from 1958 the Ho Chi Minh trail through Laos carried supplies, and by 1961 North Vietnamese soldiers were being sent south. President Kennedy sent military advisers and aid; in 1963 Diệm was killed in a coup by his own army, which the United States backed.

After the Gulf of Tonkin incident of 1964, Congress allowed President Johnson to expand the American role without declaring war. He began bombing the North and sent combat troops: 184,000 by 1966 and 536,000 by 1969. The Tet Offensive of 1968, a military defeat for the communists, turned more Americans against the war. From 1969 President Nixon pursued 'Vietnamization', handing the fighting to the South Vietnamese army as American troops withdrew; the war spread into Cambodia after a coup there in 1970.

The last American forces left after the Paris Peace Accords of 1973. The North broke the accords, and its 1975 Spring Offensive overran the South; Saigon fell on 30 April 1975, and the country was reunified as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam in 1976, while Laos and Cambodia also became communist. Estimates of Vietnamese dead range from 970,000 to 3 million, with some 275,000-310,000 Cambodians, 20,000-62,000 Laotians and 58,220 American service members killed; the war was marked by massacres such as Huế and Mỹ Lai and by the spraying of toxic herbicides over a fifth of South Vietnam's jungle.

Q8683.title: Cold War
paras: The Cold War was the geopolitical rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies, the capitalist Western Bloc and the communist Eastern Bloc, from the end of the Second World War until the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. It was 'cold' because the two superpowers never fought each other directly; they backed opposing sides in proxy wars and competed through an arms race in conventional and nuclear weapons, the space race, espionage, propaganda, embargoes and even sport. The writer George Orwell used the term 'cold war' in a 1945 essay.

After 1945 the Soviet Union installed satellite governments in Eastern Europe and North Korea, dividing Europe and Germany by an 'Iron Curtain'. American policy was 'containment', set out by the diplomat George Kennan and declared as the Truman Doctrine in 1947; the Marshall Plan of 1948 helped rebuild Western Europe and NATO was founded in 1949, matched by the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact in 1955. In 1949 the Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb and the communist People's Republic of China was founded. Early confrontations were the Berlin Blockade of 1948-1949 and the Korean War of 1950-1953.

As colonies won independence, many became battlefields of the Cold War, and both powers used aid to court non-aligned states. The Cuban Revolution of 1959 created the first communist government in the Western Hemisphere, and the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 is widely seen as the closest the world came to nuclear war. The Soviet Union crushed the Hungarian Revolution in 1956 and led the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968; the Vietnam War of 1955-1975 ended in North Vietnamese victory; and the Soviet Union and China fell out by 1961, coming close to war in 1969.

In the 1970s 'détente' brought American contacts with China from 1972 and treaties limiting nuclear arsenals, but the fall of US-allied governments in Iran and Nicaragua and the Soviet war in Afghanistan from 1979 raised tensions again. Mikhail Gorbachev, Soviet leader from 1985, widened political freedoms, which helped bring about the revolutions of 1989 in Eastern Europe and the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, ending the Cold War.

Q8736.title: Treaty of Versailles
paras: The Treaty of Versailles, signed in the Palace of Versailles on 28 June 1919, exactly five years after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, ended the state of war between Germany and most of the Allied powers. The other Central Powers signed separate treaties. It was drafted at the Paris Peace Conference, which opened in January 1919 with nearly thirty nations taking part but was dominated by the 'Big Four': Britain, France, the United States and Italy. Germany was not allowed to take part in the negotiations.

The treaty required Germany to disarm, to give up territory, to hand over alleged war criminals, to agree to the trial of the former Kaiser, to recognise the independence of states carved from lands of the German Empire and to pay reparations. Danzig and the Saarland were placed under the League of Nations, whose founding covenant was part of the treaty, and France was allowed to exploit the Saar's coal until 1935. In Article 231, the 'war guilt' clause, Germany accepted responsibility for the loss and damage caused by the war, the basis of the reparations.

It satisfied no one. John Maynard Keynes called it a 'Carthaginian peace', too harsh on Germany; Marshal Foch thought it far too lenient; historians still debate it. Germany was neither reconciled nor permanently weakened. In the United States, President Woodrow Wilson's League was opposed in the Senate, by 'irreconcilables' and by 'reservationists' under Henry Cabot Lodge, and on 19 March 1920 the treaty fell seven votes short of ratification; the United States made a separate peace with Germany and never joined the League.

Its problems led to the Locarno Treaties, which eased relations in Europe, and the reparations were rescheduled and reduced by the Dawes and Young Plans. Bitter resentment of the treaty in Germany fed the rise of the Nazi Party.

Q486.title: Chernobyl disaster
Q486.place: Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant, near Pripyat, Ukrainian SSR (Soviet Union)
paras: On 26 April 1986 reactor 4 of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant, near Pripyat in the Ukrainian SSR, exploded during a test. The United Nations' scientific committee on radiation (UNSCEAR) calls it the most serious accident ever to occur in the nuclear power industry; it is one of only two accidents, with Fukushima in 2011, rated at the maximum level of the International Nuclear Event Scale.

The operators were running a test that simulated cooling the reactor during a power blackout, after an accidental drop in reactor power. When they shut down the reactor in an unstable state, flaws in its design (an RBMK, moderated by graphite) caused a huge, uncontrollable power surge. The reactor ruptured and lost its coolant, steam explosions and a meltdown destroyed the reactor building, and a fire in the core spread radioactive material, mainly iodine-131 and caesium isotopes, across the Soviet Union and Europe.

Two workers were killed by the explosion. Acute radiation syndrome was confirmed in 134 of the plant staff and emergency workers, and 28 of them died within a few months. The Soviet government did not acknowledge the accident publicly until two days later, when raised radiation was detected in Sweden. About 115,000 people were evacuated from around the reactor in 1986, starting with a 10-kilometre zone 36 hours after the accident that was later widened to 30 kilometres, and about 220,000 more were relocated in later years from Belarus, Russia and Ukraine.

Children who drank milk contaminated with radioactive iodine received heavy doses to the thyroid: more than 6,000 cases of thyroid cancer had been reported among those exposed as children and adolescents by 2005, with about 15 deaths. UNSCEAR found no strong evidence of other increases in cancer attributable to the accident. The response involved more than half a million people.
